title: Why solving a real problem isn't enough: a viability model from problem to business model
summary: Jason Cohen explains why many startups fail despite a real problem and a working product. He lays out a chain of filters (Plausible, Self-Aware, Lucrative, Liquid, Eager, Enduring) and a multiplicative Fermi-estimate score to test viability, plus exceptions and how niching can fix a bad score.

principles.text: Solving a real problem is not enough to build a company; many failures had a real problem and a product that worked.
principles.quote: These companies fail because solving a problem is--perhaps surprisingly--not nearly enough to build a successful company.

principles.text: Funnel math sets minimum market size: ~1% click and ~1% pay means ~10M impressions for 1,000 customers, so you need ~10M consumers or ~100k businesses.
Customers who don't know or care they have the problem won't search for or buy a solution; you can't force a market.
principles.quote: If a person does not already believe they have a problem, they will not be surfing the internet looking for a solution, and even if they happen upon your website somehow, you cannot get them to spend money to solve a problem they don't think they have.

principles.text: Consumers rarely pay; self-funded companies should target businesses, who spend to solve problems and to make money.
principles.quote: In general, consumers don't like paying for stuff, hence the multi-trillion-dollar success of having people "pay" with attention (advertisement) and data (privacy).

principles.text: Lock-in, contracts and bundling can block a sale regardless of product quality or price; build lock-in that protects you from competitors.
principles.quote: Notice that **all these forces have nothing to do with your product or its price**.

principles.text: Targeting a niche often yields a better business model, since it can raise willingness, budget and urgency even as it shrinks the customer count.
principles.quote: **targeting a niche often results in a better business model**, because although it reduces the number of target customers, it can increase several other numbers.
